words.definition: An agent that triggers or speeds up a reaction or event while remaining unchanged itself.
words.example: The factory closure was the catalyst for the town's slow economic decline.
words.mnemonic: In chemistry a catalyst speeds a reaction — picture a 'cat' pouncing to set everything in motion.

words.definition: To bring about an event abruptly or sooner than it would otherwise have occurred.
words.example: A single careless remark precipitated a full-blown diplomatic crisis.
words.mnemonic: Rain (precipitation) falls suddenly from clouds — to precipitate is to make something fall or happen suddenly.

words.definition: To give rise to or bring into existence a feeling, condition, or situation.
words.example: His steady honesty engendered trust among even his fiercest rivals.
words.mnemonic: Root 'gen' means birth or create (as in 'generate', 'genesis') — to engender is to birth something into being.

words.definition: To produce offspring or generate something, especially in large numbers.
words.example: The hit movie spawned a dozen cheap imitations within a single year.
words.mnemonic: Fish spawn thousands of eggs at once — spawn means to churn out many.

words.definition: To deliberately stir someone into a strong reaction, often anger.
words.example: She kept poking fun at him, clearly trying to provoke a fight.
words.mnemonic: Think 'pro-poke' — you keep poking someone until they finally react.

words.definition: To urge or stir people toward violent or disorderly action.
words.example: The speaker was arrested for inciting the crowd to riot.
words.mnemonic: Incite sounds like 'ignite' — you set a crowd on fire to make it act.

words.definition: To set a harmful action or scheme in motion.
words.example: Two students instigated the walkout that emptied every classroom by noon.
words.mnemonic: In-STIG-ate: picture a 'stig' poking a fire with a stick to start trouble.

words.definition: To promote the growth of unrest, rebellion, or bad feeling.
words.example: Foreign agents worked quietly to foment rebellion in the border provinces.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'ferment' — foment stirs up unrest the way yeast bubbles and ferments.

words.definition: To set alight, or to awaken a feeling, interest, or passion.
words.example: A single encouraging teacher kindled her lifelong love of physics.
words.mnemonic: A Kindle e-reader lights up — kindle means to light a fire or spark a feeling.

words.definition: To urge someone or something onward to greater effort or action.
words.example: The looming deadline spurred the team to finish in record time.
words.mnemonic: Cowboy spurs dig into a horse to make it run faster — to spur is to urge on.

words.definition: To draw out a response, answer, or fact from someone.
words.example: The comedian's dry jokes elicited roars of laughter from the audience.
words.mnemonic: A detective 'e-licits' a confession — draws it out (not 'illicit', meaning illegal).

words.definition: To call a memory, image, or feeling to mind.
words.example: The smell of pine needles evoked childhood Christmases at her grandmother's house.
words.mnemonic: E + 'voke' (voice) — evoke 'calls out' a memory so the past seems to speak.

words.definition: To persuade someone to act, or to bring about a condition.
words.example: No bribe could induce the guard to unlock the gate.
words.mnemonic: In + 'duce' (to lead) — you lead someone into doing something; a doctor induces labor.

words.definition: To follow or occur afterward, especially as a consequence.
words.example: He knocked over the candle, and chaos ensued within seconds.
words.mnemonic: En + 'sue' — once you sue someone, a long process follows; it ensues.

words.definition: To reach a climax or final decisive point after a gradual buildup.
words.example: Years of grueling training culminated in a gold medal at the Olympics.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'culmen', meaning summit — to culminate is to reach the peak of a mountain.

words.definition: To involve or make necessary as a natural or unavoidable part of something.
words.example: Adopting a puppy will entail early-morning walks and plenty of patience.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'in-tail' — owning a dog comes attached to responsibilities, like the wagging tail is attached to the dog.

words.definition: To bring into existence, to cause, or to father a child.
words.example: Violence tends to beget more violence, spiraling on until someone chooses to stop.
words.mnemonic: Break it as 'be-get' — you 'be' the one who 'gets' you offspring or a result.

words.definition: To produce or provide something as a product, profit, or result.
words.example: The old apple tree can still yield a surprising number of fruit each autumn.
words.mnemonic: Picture the red 'YIELD' road sign — you give way, handing something over to what follows.

words.definition: To produce offspring, or to cause something to develop and spread.
words.example: Neglect and boredom can breed resentment among even the most loyal employees.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'seed' — plant a seed and it multiplies, just as breeding makes more.

words.definition: A complicated or often unwelcome result that follows from an action or decision.
words.example: The lawyers spent hours mapping every ramification of the merger before anyone signed.
words.mnemonic: Root 'ram-' is Latin for branch (ramus) — effects branching out like limbs from a tree.

words.definition: An unintended, usually harmful effect that follows an event or action.
words.example: He hadn't considered the repercussion of skipping the meeting until his boss called that night.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'percuss' — like a drum's percussion, the hit of an action echoes and reverberates back.

words.definition: A result or effect produced by an earlier action or condition.
words.example: Missing the deadline had one clear consequence: the project lost its funding.
words.mnemonic: Split as 'con-sequence' — what comes next in the sequence after something happens.

words.definition: The situation or period following a significant, often destructive, event.
words.example: In the aftermath of the flood, neighbors gathered to shovel mud from each other's homes.
words.mnemonic: 'after' + 'math' (an old word for a mowing) — the second growth left after the harvest is cut.

words.definition: The final result or conclusion of a series of events.
words.example: They argued for weeks, but the upshot was that nobody changed their vote.
words.mnemonic: Think of the deciding final 'up shot' in archery — the last arrow that settles the whole match.

words.definition: The harmful side effects or results that follow an event or decision.
words.example: The political fallout from the scandal cost three ministers their jobs within a month.
words.mnemonic: Radioactive dust that 'falls out' of the sky after a blast — the damaging debris that settles afterward.

words.definition: A strong, hostile public reaction against a decision, idea, or change.
words.example: The company faced fierce backlash after removing the beloved feature overnight.
words.mnemonic: A whip that 'lashes back' — the recoil that strikes the one who swung it.

words.definition: A force or influence that makes something happen or move forward.
words.example: Her sister's recovery gave her the impetus to finally start running again.
words.mnemonic: Same root as 'impact' and 'impetuous' — a forceful push driving you into motion.

words.definition: Something that rouses activity, energy, or a response.
words.example: A cup of strong coffee is the only stimulus that gets him talking before noon.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'stimulus' was a pointed stick for prodding cattle — it pokes you into action.

words.definition: A factor that decides or strongly shapes how something turns out.
words.example: Family income proved to be the single largest determinant of the students' test scores.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'termin' (Latin terminus, an end or boundary) — it fixes where things end up.

words.definition: A thing or event that comes before another and often leads to it.
words.example: Historians see the long drought as the antecedent to the great migration that followed.
words.mnemonic: 'ante-' (before) + 'ced-' (go, as in precede) — literally that which goes before.

words.definition: Something that comes before and leads to the development of another thing.
words.example: The clunky mechanical calculator was a precursor to the modern computer.
words.mnemonic: Latin pre- (before) + cursor (runner) — the runner who goes ahead of the pack.

words.definition: A person or thing that signals the approach of something about to happen.
words.example: The first robin of spring is often seen as a harbinger of warmer days.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'har-BRINGER' — the one who brings the news ahead of time.

words.definition: A sign or warning that something important, often bad, is likely to happen.
words.example: The sudden darkening of the sky felt like a portent of the storm ahead.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'PORT-tent' — a dark tent pitched at the harbor, ominous and looming.

words.definition: To announce or be a sign of something that is coming.
words.example: Cheerful advertisements began to herald the launch of the new phone weeks early.
words.mnemonic: A royal 'herald' blew a trumpet to announce the king — think headline news bearer.

words.definition: Relating to a relationship where one thing directly produces or brings about another.
words.example: Researchers established a causal link between smoking and the rise in lung disease.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'cause' — causal is the adjective for a genuine cause-and-effect tie.

words.definition: Depending on something else that is not yet certain to happen.
words.example: Her promotion is contingent on the company meeting its sales targets this quarter.
words.mnemonic: Think 'con-TINGE-ent' — the outcome is tinged by, and hangs on, another condition.

words.definition: To have a mutual connection in which two things tend to change together.
words.example: Studies show that hours of sleep closely correlate with students' test scores.
words.mnemonic: co- (together) + 'relate' — two things relating together, moving in step.

words.definition: To regard something as being caused by or belonging to a particular source.
words.example: Critics ascribe the film's success to its unforgettable soundtrack rather than its plot.
words.mnemonic: a- + 'scribe' (write) — you write a cause down against someone's name.

words.definition: To say that something was caused or created by a specific person or thing.
words.example: Historians attribute the empire's collapse to years of unchecked corruption.
words.mnemonic: at- + 'tribute' — you pay tribute to the source you say is responsible.

words.definition: To claim that someone is responsible for a fault or wrongdoing.
words.example: The lawyer tried to impute the accident to the driver's carelessness, not the weather.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'im-PUTE' — to 'put' blame onto someone unfairly.

words.definition: To cause something to start or happen suddenly.
words.example: A single careless spark can trigger a wildfire across the dry hills.
words.mnemonic: Picture pulling a gun's trigger — one small pull sets off a big event.

words.definition: To cause someone to take action or to make something occur.
words.example: The rising ticket prices prompted many fans to watch the game from home.
words.mnemonic: A theater 'prompter' whispers a cue that moves the actor to speak.

words.definition: To produce or bring something into existence.
words.example: The new turbines can generate enough electricity to power ten thousand homes.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'genesis' and 'generator' — the origin that makes things exist.

words.definition: To make something harmful or unpleasant less severe.
words.example: Planting trees along the riverbank helped mitigate the damage from seasonal floods.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'mighty-gate' — a strong gate that softens the blow of a flood.

words.definition: To make a bad situation, problem, or feeling worse.
words.example: Ignoring the small leak only exacerbated the water damage in the basement.
words.mnemonic: Think 'egg-zaggerate' — blowing a problem up bigger, making it worse.

words.definition: To make a bad situation or condition more serious or severe.
words.example: Scratching the rash will only aggravate it and slow the healing.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'a grave' — make things bad enough and you're digging one.

words.definition: To make pain or a problem less severe or easier to bear.
words.example: A cold compress helped alleviate the swelling after her fall.
words.mnemonic: Say 'a-LEV-iate' — 'lev' means light (Latin levis); it lightens your load.

words.definition: To make an unsatisfactory condition better or more tolerable.
words.example: New drainage ameliorated the flooding that once ruined the low fields.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'a-MEAL-iorate' — a good meal makes everything better; 'melior' is Latin for better.

words.definition: To make a difficulty worse by adding further problems to it.
words.example: Missing the deadline compounded the team's already mounting troubles.
words.mnemonic: A chemical compound piles parts together — here you pile more onto a mess.

words.definition: To increase the strength, size, or impact of something.
words.example: The stadium speakers amplified the singer's voice across the whole crowd.
words.mnemonic: An 'amp' (amplifier) makes sound bigger — add amps to anything.

words.definition: To make an object appear larger, or to increase the degree of something.
words.example: Under the lens, the magnified cells revealed tiny hidden structures.
words.mnemonic: A magnifying glass makes things huge; 'magn' is Latin for great or large.

words.definition: To make something stronger, more extreme, or more concentrated.
words.example: The storm intensified overnight and uprooted trees by dawn.
words.mnemonic: Break it to 'in-tense' — muscles grow tense as pressure keeps building.

words.definition: To make or become smaller, weaker, or less in amount.
words.example: Her fears diminished as the plane leveled off and the ride smoothed out.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'mini' inside it — something is being shrunk to mini size.

words.definition: To cut short or reduce the extent, amount, or duration of something.
words.example: Budget cuts forced the library to curtail its weekend hours.
words.mnemonic: 'Curt' + 'tail' — cut the tail off to make it short and curt.

words.definition: To make progress or action slow or difficult.
words.example: Thick fog hindered the rescue team's climb up the ridge.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'hind' (behind) — it holds you back and keeps you behind.

words.definition: To slow or block the movement or progress of something.
words.example: Debris on the tracks impeded the train for over an hour.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'pede' = foot (Latin) — something grabs your feet and slows you.

words.definition: To restrict or interfere with someone's freedom to move or act.
words.example: A heavy backpack hampered his sprint to the finish line.
words.mnemonic: Picture a laundry hamper strapped to your legs — it holds you back.

words.definition: To prevent someone from accomplishing a plan or purpose.
words.example: Alert guards thwarted the thieves before they reached the vault.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'thwack!' — a blow that stops a scheme dead in its tracks.

words.definition: To hold back, smother, or keep something from being expressed.
words.example: She stifled a yawn during the long, dull lecture.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'stuffy' — a stuffy, airless room smothers you.

words.definition: To forcibly restrain, put down, or keep something from being expressed.
words.example: The regime tried to suppress every report of the protest.
words.mnemonic: 'Sub' (down) + 'press' — press it down and hold it under.

words.definition: To stop or suppress something, especially unrest or a strong emotion.
words.example: The mayor called in officers to quell the riot before it spread downtown.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'quench' — you quell a rebellion the way you quench a fire.

words.definition: To bring under control, often by force or authority.
words.example: It took three guards to subdue the struggling suspect.
words.mnemonic: 'sub' (under) + 'due' — force someone under, and they are now 'sub-dued'.

words.definition: To prevent something bad from happening, or to turn away.
words.example: Quick thinking by the pilot averted a mid-air collision.
words.mnemonic: a-VERT sounds like 'divert' — you divert the danger away.

words.definition: To prevent something by taking action ahead of time.
words.example: She paid the invoice early to forestall any late fees.
words.mnemonic: 'fore' (before) + 'stall' — you stall it before it can even start.

words.definition: To make something impossible or shut it out in advance.
words.example: A serious criminal record may preclude you from many government jobs.
words.mnemonic: 'pre' (before) + 'clude' (close) — the door is closed before you arrive.

words.definition: To discourage someone from acting, usually through fear of consequences.
words.example: Bright porch lights can deter burglars from approaching a house.
words.mnemonic: Hidden in 'deterrent' — picture a 'detour' sign that scares you off the road.

words.definition: To talk someone out of doing something.
words.example: Her friends tried to dissuade her from quitting such a stable job.
words.mnemonic: 'dis' (opposite) + 'suade' (persuade) — literally the opposite of persuade.

words.definition: To shock or excite people into taking sudden action.
words.example: The tragedy galvanized the neighborhood into forming a nightly safety patrol.
words.mnemonic: Galvani jolted frog legs with electricity — to galvanize is to jolt a crowd into motion.

words.definition: To push or drive something forward.
words.example: A strong tailwind propelled the little sailboat across the bay.
words.mnemonic: Think 'propeller' — a propeller pushes a plane forward.

words.definition: To increase rapidly and spread in great numbers.
words.example: Coffee shops have proliferated on nearly every corner of the city.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'prolific' — a prolific breeder produces offspring that multiply fast.

words.definition: To begin to grow or expand quickly and flourish.
words.example: Her weekend side hustle burgeoned into a full-time business within a year.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'bulge on' — a bud that bulges outward and bursts into bloom.

words.definition: To increase rapidly in intensity, size, or seriousness.
words.example: A minor disagreement over parking quickly escalated into a shouting match.
words.mnemonic: Think 'escalator' — it carries things steadily upward.

words.definition: To gradually decrease in strength, size, or intensity.
words.example: As the long night wore on, my enthusiasm for the party began to wane.
words.mnemonic: The moon wanes — picture 'wan', pale fading light growing thinner.

words.definition: To become steadily smaller in size or amount.
words.example: Their savings dwindled after months without any steady work.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'whittle down' — whittling a stick smaller and smaller.

words.definition: To become less intense, or to reduce in amount.
words.example: We huddled on the porch until the storm finally abated.
words.mnemonic: Related to 'bated breath' — bring the intensity down, hold it back.

words.definition: To grow calmer or settle to a lower level after a period of intensity.
words.example: After the storm passed, the floodwaters slowly began to subside.
words.mnemonic: sub- (down) + -side: picture things sinking DOWN and settling to the SIDE until they're quiet.

words.definition: To scatter or fade away until nothing is left.
words.example: The crowd's excitement dissipated once the band canceled the encore.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'dizzy-pate' — a dizzy head whose thoughts scatter and drift off in every direction.

words.definition: To build up gradually over time, especially interest or benefits.
words.example: By leaving the deposit untouched, she let years of interest accrue in the account.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'a crew' — a crew that keeps growing as more members steadily sign on.

words.definition: To gather a growing quantity of something over a stretch of time.
words.example: Dust tends to accumulate on shelves that no one ever bothers to clean.
words.mnemonic: ac-CUMULO-late: think of cumulus clouds piling higher and heavier in the sky.

words.definition: To force someone into an action through pressure or authority.
words.example: The judge can compel a reluctant witness to testify by issuing a subpoena.
words.mnemonic: com- + Latin 'pellere' (to push): someone is pushed completely into doing it.

words.definition: To make someone act by using threats or intimidation.
words.example: The gang tried to coerce local shop owners into paying for 'protection.'
words.mnemonic: Hear 'co-ERASE' — a bully threatening to ERASE you unless you give in.

words.definition: To hold back or restrict within fixed limits.
words.example: A tight budget constrained the team to only the most essential purchases.
words.mnemonic: con- + STRAIN: imagine a chain that STRAINS tight and keeps you from moving.

words.definition: To make something required or unavoidable.
words.example: The sudden pipe leak necessitated an emergency call to the plumber.
words.mnemonic: Root is 'necessity' — the thing turns an option into a must-do.

words.definition: To make a process easier or help it run smoothly.
words.example: A skilled moderator can facilitate the debate so even quiet members get heard.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'facilis' (easy — same root as 'facile'): you smooth the way.

words.definition: To give someone the means or opportunity to do something.
words.example: A generous scholarship enabled her to attend college without any debt.
words.mnemonic: en- + ABLE: literally to make someone ABLE to act.

words.definition: To move quickly or cause something to happen sooner.
words.example: She hastened to the platform, terrified of missing the last train home.
words.mnemonic: HASTE + -en: to add haste to something.

words.definition: To increase speed or make something progress faster.
words.example: The driver accelerated the moment the traffic light turned green.
words.mnemonic: The ACCELERATOR pedal in a car — press it and everything speeds up.

words.definition: To speed up the progress of a task or process.
words.example: For an extra fee, the agency will expedite your passport application.
words.mnemonic: Latin ex-ped (free the feet): unshackle the feet so a job races ahead — like EXPRESS delivery.

words.definition: To draw something out so it lasts much longer than needed.
words.example: The lawyers protracted the trial with endless motions and objections.
words.mnemonic: pro- + TRACT (to pull/drag): like a TRACTOR dragging something out far longer.

words.definition: To make something continue for a greater span of time.
words.example: They prolonged their vacation by an extra week when the weather stayed warm.
words.mnemonic: pro- + LONG: to stretch something out and make it LONGer.
